facts.fact: Water utilities add chlorine or chloramine to tap water to kill harmful microorganisms.
Chloramine is a longer-lasting relative of chlorine and is harder to spot.
For fish and other aquatic life, even a slight trace of chlorine can be fatal.
Chloramine forms when chlorine and ammonia are combined, and it is very toxic to fish and other aquatic organisms.
Chloramine is toxic to both freshwater and saltwater fish.
Chlorine kills the beneficial filter bacteria, which can cause pollution spikes and make fish sick.
Chlorine can damage delicate gill membranes, and sensitive species can die from it.
Most liquid dechlorinators contain sodium thiosulphate, which turns chlorine into chloride.
Most dechlorinators neutralize chlorine in about two minutes and chloramine in about five.
Some dechlorinators cannot neutralize chloramine at all, so check the label.
Without a dechlorinator, chlorine can be driven off by heavy aeration in a bucket for at least 12 hours.
A UF/IFAS classroom activity compares two methods: sodium thiosulfate neutralizer, which should leave no measurable chlorine, and vigorous aeration for 24 hours.
Seachem Prime dose: 1 capful (5 mL) per 200 L (50 US gal) of new water. Each cap thread is about 1 mL for smaller volumes.
Seachem says Prime removes chlorine and chloramine, detoxifies heavy metals at tap-water levels, and does not change pH.
With very high chloramine levels, Seachem says a double dose of Prime is safe.
Seachem says to use a half dose of Prime if water is above 30 °C (86 °F) and chlorine or ammonia is low.
Seachem says Prime binds ammonia, nitrite and nitrate into a non-toxic form but does not remove them. The biofilter still has to process them.
Pure sodium thiosulfate neutralizes the chlorine part of chloramine but leaves the ammonia, so ammonia needs to be monitored or bound with another product.
About 2.5 parts ascorbic acid (vitamin C) neutralize 1 part chlorine.
At the concentrations used for dechlorination, vitamin C is not toxic to aquatic life.
A vitamin C solution breaks down within one to two days, so mix it fresh.
Chloramine in water for fish should be kept below 0.1 mg/L.
Add the dechlorinator to the new water before it goes into the tank. If you dose straight into the tank, dose for the whole tank volume.
Follow the dosing instructions of the brand you use.
Skipping dechlorination is a mistake. Claims that it is unnecessary come from a lack of understanding.
Boiling the water, adding salt or letting it stand in an open container does not remove chloramine.
Nessler-based liquid ammonia test kits give false readings after Prime is used. Seachem suggests its own ammonia kit or waiting, because Prime dissipates within about 24 hours.
Practical Fishkeeping says the worry that dechlorinator additives coat or smother fish gills is unfounded.
Practical Fishkeeping says dechlorinators are harmless to fish except at 'ludicrous' doses.
Practical Fishkeeping says to treat 'stress relief' claims on dechlorinators with caution.
A sulfur smell and occasional small black specks in Prime are normal, and the product does not expire if stored properly.
Vietnam's drinking-water standard (QCVN 01-1/BYT) requires free residual chlorine of 0.2–1.0 mg/L at suppliers that disinfect with chlorine, so tap water reaching the home still contains chlorine.
QCVN 01-1:2018/BYT (Thông tư 41/2018/TT-BYT) has been replaced by QCVN 01-1:2024/BYT (Thông tư 52/2024/TT-BYT), which keeps free residual chlorine at 0.2–1.0 mg/L.
In Vietnam, dechlorinating solutions such as Fresh Booster are sold as a way to avoid aging tap water in the sun ('phơi nước') or aerating it to drive off chlorine.
